title: The Second World War
hookLine: Sikhs fought in Italy, Burma and North Africa

lines: A TIN BOX ON A HIGH SHELF.
A MEDAL, A BADGE, A REGIMENT.
cards: Some families keep a tin box on a high shelf, brought down only when a grandchild asks. Inside: a medal on a faded ribbon, a cap badge, a folded paper with a regiment's name on it.
In some Sikh families the man those things belonged to is a grandfather or a great-grandfather, and the box has moved house with them, from a village in Punjab to Delhi, or Birmingham, or Toronto.
A generation after the trenches, war came again. And Sikhs went again: into the deserts of North Africa, up the mountains of Italy, and through the jungles of Burma.

teach.b: First, the second call. The fathers had come home from France and Mesopotamia, or had not. Now their sons enlisted in the Indian Army for a new war, and Sikhs served alongside Hindus, Muslims and others.
Second, three landscapes. North Africa was sand, heat and thirst. Italy was rivers and steep hillsides, taken one ridge at a time.
Burma was rain, mud and forest so thick you could lose the man in front of you. Same turbans, same Ardas, a different world each time. Third, the measure.

At Ang 1105 of the Guru Granth Sahib, a verse of Kabir names the true warrior: the one who fights for the sake of deen, a word some translators render the helpless and others the faith, and who, though cut to pieces, never leaves the field.
Some readers hear a battlefield in it; others hear the fight inside a person, against anger and greed. The verse can hold both.
Sikhs have a name for an ideal that joins them, sant-sipahi, the saint-soldier: someone whose bravery is held inside devotion and restraint.
Fourth, the generation. The young men in those photographs came home to a country about to be divided, which is where this story goes next.
To some grandchildren they were old men at the gurdwara, or in a chair by the window, and only the box on the shelf remembers them young.

how: Some Sikh families keep photographs and medals of relatives who served in the Second World War, and some gurdwaras and community groups mark remembrance days for Sikh soldiers.

o: a holy man who refuses ever to carry arms
a soldier who sets faith aside to fight a war
a saint-soldier: bravery held inside devotion

games.q: the second call — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir's verse at Ang 1105 calls anyone who fights a true warrior
he names the one who fights for the sake of the helpless and never leaves the field.
Sikhs served in the Second World War alongside Hindus, Muslims and others
they served together in the Indian Army.
the war kept Sikh soldiers on a single front
they served in North Africa, Italy and Burma.

games.q: you're a young Sikh soldier on a new front. a verse of Kabir at Ang 1105 gives a measure for the true warrior. which one is it?
o: one who fights for the helpless, and never leaves the field.
games.why: Kabir names the one who fights for the sake of the helpless and, cut to pieces, never leaves the field. some readers hear the fight inside a person too.

practice: Bring to mind your grandparents' generation: your own grandparents if you knew them, or the old people of your street, your temple, your town.

Whatever they lived through, they were young once and afraid once, so breathe in and picture one of them at twenty, and breathe out giving them a little of the attention they may never have asked for.
If you pray, Waheguru can go with that breath.

wordCard.voice: Sant-sipahi, saint-soldier, bravery held inside devotion and restraint: a generation after the trenches, Sikh soldiers served again, in North Africa, Italy and Burma. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they served again. The same turbans, a different world. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.
